title: Why Do Icebreakers Climb On Top of the Ice?
description:
Most people imagine an icebreaker smashing through ice like a hammer, or cutting it like a knife. It does neither. An icebreaker drives up onto the ice, and then crushes it with its own weight, again and again, thousands of times a day. Today, ten parts of an icebreaker, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:01 1. The sloped bow
2:04 2. The ice belt
3:10 3. The round hull
4:16 4. The heeling tanks
5:15 5. The air bubbling system
6:16 6. The electric drive
7:20 7. The nuclear reactor
8:27 8. The backward ship
9:31 9. The towing notch
10:27 10. The sideways icebreaker
11:29 The verdict

Sources:
- Icebreaker hull form, ice belt, heeling system, air bubbling system, diesel-electric propulsion: Wikipedia, "Icebreaker" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icebreaker
- Fram and Fridtjof Nansen: Wikipedia, "Fram" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fram
- Nuclear icebreakers Lenin (1957) and Arktika (North Pole, 1977): Wikipedia, "Lenin (1957 icebreaker)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenin_(1957_icebreaker) and "Arktika (1972 icebreaker)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arktika_(1972_icebreaker)
- Double acting ships: Wikipedia, "Double acting ship" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_acting_ship
- Towing notch: Wikipedia, "Icebreaker" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icebreaker
- Oblique icebreaker Baltika: Wikipedia, "Baltika (icebreaker)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltika_(icebreaker)
- Low temperature steels and ice class rules: Wikipedia, "Ice class" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_class
